parts.context: A brother and sister are discussing a problem involving their elderly father’s computer.

lines: Tomasz, it’s me. Are you sitting down? Dad called me an hour ago, and he was really shaken up.

He’s fine physically. But yesterday afternoon he got a pop-up on his computer saying it was infected, with a phone number to call. He called it, and the man on the line convinced him to install a program so he could ‘clean’ the computer remotely.
Oh no. Let me guess. Then he asked for payment.

Four hundred dollars, which Dad paid with his credit card. And while the man was supposedly fixing things, he had complete control of the screen for almost an hour. Dad says he saw the online banking page open at one point, but he assumed it was part of the repair.
Has anything actually gone missing from his account?

Not that we can see yet. I drove over this morning, and we called the bank together. They froze his online access and cancelled the credit card. The bank thinks the four hundred may be recoverable as a fraudulent charge, but they couldn’t promise anything.
That’s something, at least. How’s he taking it?

Embarrassed, mostly. He kept saying, ‘I should have known better.’ He’s refusing to touch the computer now. Which would be fine, except he does all his banking and his video calls with the grandkids on it.
And the program is presumably still installed?
I unplugged the computer from the internet before I left, but I didn’t know what else to do. That’s why I’m calling you. You’re the one who does this for a living.

qs.q: What did the caller persuade their father to do?
o: Give his banking password over the phone
Buy gift cards to pay for a computer repair
Let a stranger control his computer from a distance
Bring his computer into a repair shop for a full cleaning
qs.ev: install a program so he could ‘clean’ the computer remotely
qs.x: The program let the man control the screen “remotely” for almost an hour. Payment was by credit card, not gift cards, and no password was given by phone.

qs.q: What has the bank done so far?
o: Blocked his online banking and his card
Returned the four hundred dollars to his account right away
Confirmed that money was taken from his savings
Asked Hana to report the scam to the police
qs.ev: They froze his online access and cancelled the credit card.
qs.x: The bank froze online access and cancelled the card. It only thinks the $400 “may be recoverable”, with no promise, and nothing has been confirmed missing.

qs.q: How does their father feel about what happened?
o: Angry at the bank for not warning him sooner
Worried that his grandchildren were affected too
Determined to report the man to the police himself
Ashamed that he was fooled
qs.ev: I should have known better.
qs.x: He is “embarrassed” and blames himself for not knowing better. The grandchildren are mentioned only because he uses the computer for video calls with them.

lines: Okay. First things first: that computer needs to be completely wiped and reinstalled. Even if we uninstall the program, there could be something else hidden on it.
Can you do that this weekend?
Saturday, yes. But I’m more worried about what happens next time. Someone’s going to call him again. These people share lists of who fell for it.
I was thinking we could just replace the computer with a tablet. Fewer pop-ups, simpler apps.

A tablet would help with the pop-ups, but it wouldn’t stop a phone call from a fake bank. And you know Dad. He types his letters to the newspaper with two fingers on a full keyboard. He’d hate a touch screen.

True. He’d probably stop writing to the editor altogether, and then where would the newspaper be? What about that remote monitoring software you mentioned once? Where you can see his screen from your place?

I could set that up. But honestly, I’m uneasy about it. It means I can see everything he does, his emails, his banking, all of it. He’s eighty-one, not a child. I wouldn’t want to be watched like that, and I doubt he would either.
Fair enough. So what would actually protect him without treating him like a kid?

Two things, I think. One: set up his bank account so that any payment over a certain amount sends a text to one of us as well as to him. Two: he needs a simple rule, written down next to the computer, saying that no real company will ever ask him to call a number on a pop-up.

qs.q: Why does Tomasz think wiping the computer is necessary?
o: Their father wants a completely new system installed
Removing the program alone might not be enough
The bank requires it before restoring his access
The scammer may still be watching the screen now
qs.ev: there could be something else hidden on it
qs.x: Even after uninstalling the program, other harmful software could remain hidden. The computer is already unplugged, so the scammer cannot be watching, and the bank sets no such condition.

qs.q: Why does Tomasz reject the tablet idea?
o: It would cost more than repairing the old computer
Tablets are more open to fake pop-up messages
Their father has never once used a touch-screen device
It solves only part of the problem and suits him poorly
qs.ev: it wouldn’t stop a phone call from a fake bank
qs.x: A tablet would reduce pop-ups but not scam calls, and their father prefers a real keyboard. Tablets are said to have fewer pop-ups, which reverses option B.

qs.q: How does Tomasz feel about the monitoring software?
o: He thinks it would intrude on his father’s privacy
He believes it is too difficult to install from a distance
He thinks it would offer the most effective protection
He worries his father would not know how to use it
qs.ev: He’s eighty-one, not a child.
qs.x: He is “uneasy” because he could see all his father’s emails and banking, and says he would not want to be watched himself. He says he “could set that up”, so difficulty is not the issue.

lines: I like the bank alert idea. Which of us gets the texts?
Me, I suppose, since I’m usually at a desk. Although… you live ten minutes from him and I’m two hours away. If something looks wrong, you’re the one who can actually go over there.
Then put my number on it. I don’t mind.
Okay. I’ll call the bank about the alert with him on the line on Saturday, after I’ve rebuilt the computer. He has to give permission himself anyway.
Honestly, I think it’ll mean more coming from you. He listens to you. I’ll just make it sound like a lecture.
Ha. Fine. I’ll print something in big letters and tape it beside the monitor. Maybe I’ll add the bank’s real phone number at the bottom, so he has someone safe to call.
Good idea. And Hana, let’s not make a big deal of this with him. If he feels stupid, he’ll stop telling us when something strange happens, and that’s the worst outcome of all.
Agreed. I’ll just tell him we’re making his computer good as new. And I’ll bring the kids along on Saturday, so he has something to look forward to besides a lecture.
Exactly. And maybe invite him over for lunch on Sunday, so the whole weekend doesn’t feel like a repair visit.

qs.q: Who will receive the bank’s text alerts?
o: Tomasz, because he usually works at a desk
Their father only, since he must give permission
Hana, because she lives closer to their father
Both siblings, so that nothing is missed by either of them
qs.ev: Then put my number on it.
qs.x: Tomasz first offers to take the texts, then changes his mind because Hana lives ten minutes away. Their father’s permission is needed to set up the alert, but he is not the only recipient.

qs.q: Why does Tomasz want to avoid making a fuss with their father?
o: He does not want Hana to feel responsible for what happened
Their father might hide future problems from them
The bank has asked them to keep the matter private
Their father has not yet agreed to any of the changes
qs.ev: he’ll stop telling us when something strange happens
qs.x: If their father feels foolish, he may stop reporting suspicious events, which Tomasz calls the worst outcome. Nothing suggests the bank asked for secrecy.

parts.context: A student is speaking to a staff member at her college’s IT help desk.

lines: Hi. I’m hoping you can help me. I’m locked out of my student account, and I have an assignment due at midnight.
Okay, let’s see what we can do. What happens when you try to log in?
My password works, but then it asks for the code from the authenticator app. And the app was on my phone, which I left on the bus on Monday.
Ah. That’s the most common problem we see, honestly. Do you have any backup codes? When you set up two-step login, the system gives you ten one-time codes and tells you to save them.
I vaguely remember that screen. I think I clicked past it.
Most people do. All right. I can reset your two-step login, but I have to verify your identity in person first. Do you have your student card?
Thanks… That matches. Now, once I reset it, you’ll need to set up the authenticator again on a new device. Do you have a replacement phone yet?
Not until Friday. My carrier is shipping one. Can I just turn off the two-step part until then?

I’m afraid that’s not an option. The college made it mandatory for every student account last September after a wave of phishing emails. What I can do is give you a temporary access pass. It works for eight hours from the moment I issue it, and you use it instead of a code.
Eight hours. So it would run out around ten tonight?
It’s two o’clock now, so yes, ten p.m. Will that be enough time to submit?
It should be, if I go straight to the library. The assignment is mostly finished. I just need to upload it and fill in the reflection questions.
Then go straight there. And one more thing: when your new phone arrives, come back here, or use the self-service page, to register it. And this time, print those backup codes.
Believe me, I will. What happens if I miss the eight-hour window?
Then you’d need to come back during desk hours. We close at five today, and we’re not open again until nine tomorrow morning.
So no second chances tonight. Okay, I’m going. Thanks so much.

qs.q: Why can the student not log in?
o: She cannot get her second verification code
She has forgotten the password for her student account
Her account was blocked after a phishing email
Her student card has expired this semester
qs.ev: the app was on my phone, which I left on the bus on Monday
qs.x: Her password works, but the code app was on the phone she lost. Phishing emails explain why two-step login became mandatory, not why her account is locked.

qs.q: What does Reza suggest about backup codes?
o: They can only be used by staff at the help desk
They are emailed to students automatically every term
They expire if they are not used within a week
Many students fail to keep them
qs.ev: Most people do.
qs.x: When she admits clicking past the codes, “Most people do” implies this is common. The codes are given once at setup, not emailed each term.

qs.q: Why can two-step login not be switched off?
o: Her instructor requires it for every assignment uploaded online
It became a rule for all students after security problems
Her new phone must be registered before it can be removed
The temporary pass works only when it is turned on
qs.ev: The college made it mandatory for every student account last September after a wave of phishing emails.
qs.x: Two-step login is a college-wide requirement introduced after phishing attacks. Her instructor is never mentioned, and registering the new phone is a later step.

qs.q: What is the main limitation of the temporary pass?
o: It works only on computers in the college library
It must be used together with her new phone
It stops working later that evening
It can be issued only once per term to each student
qs.ev: It works for eight hours from the moment I issue it
qs.x: Issued at two o’clock, it expires at ten p.m. The library is simply where she chooses to work, and the pass replaces the code, so no phone is needed.

qs.q: What will the student most likely do next?
o: Go to the library to finish and submit her work
Wait for her replacement phone to arrive on Friday
Return to the help desk before it closes at five
Print her backup codes before uploading the assignment
qs.ev: if I go straight to the library
qs.x: She says she will go straight to the library to upload the assignment and leaves immediately. Printing codes and registering a phone happen after the new phone arrives.

parts.context: A man calls a college’s continuing education office about an online course.

lines: Hi, I registered for the online bookkeeping course that starts on the sixth, and I wanted to understand how it works before I commit. I work shifts, so my schedule’s unpredictable.

Of course. The good news is that most of the course is self-paced. The lessons are recorded, so you can watch them whenever you like. There is one live session each week, on Wednesdays at seven p.m., but it’s optional. The recordings are posted the next morning. Most students watch them on their lunch breaks or on weekends, and that seems to work well.
There are eight weekly assignments, each due Sunday at eleven fifty-nine p.m. Eastern time. Late work loses ten percent per day, up to three days. After that, it receives a zero.
Can I get an extension if I’m called in for an extra shift?
You can request one extension per course, up to five days, as long as you ask before the deadline. If you ask afterwards, the instructor isn’t allowed to grant it, even with a good reason.
Okay, so ask early. And the final exam?

The final is online but supervised. That means you’ll need a computer with a webcam and a microphone, and the proctoring software will record you for the whole two hours. You also need to show photo ID to the camera at the start. The exam is usually scheduled for the second Saturday after the last assignment.
My laptop has a camera, but it’s pretty old. Will that be a problem?

Run the system check on the course website at least a week before the exam. If your computer fails, you can book one of the exam rooms on campus instead, but those fill up quickly, so don’t leave it to the last minute.
Good to know. And if things don’t work out, what’s the refund policy?

Full refund until the end of the first week, minus a thirty-dollar administration fee. During the second week, you’ll get half the tuition back. After that, no refund, but you can transfer to the next session once, free of charge, as long as you haven’t submitted more than two assignments.
So if I fall behind in week four, I could switch to the next session rather than lose the money?
As long as you’ve handed in no more than two assignments, yes. Honestly, with a shift schedule, that’s a pretty good safety net.
That makes me feel a lot better. Thanks, Colette.

qs.q: What does Colette say about the weekly live session?
o: Students must attend at least half of the sessions to pass
It is held every Sunday evening before the deadline
It is recorded only if enough students attend
Students can miss it and watch it afterwards
qs.ev: The recordings are posted the next morning.
qs.x: The Wednesday session is optional and recordings are posted the next morning. Sunday is the assignment deadline, not the session day.

qs.q: What happens to an assignment submitted four days late?
o: It loses forty percent of its mark
It earns no marks at all
It loses ten percent of its mark
It is graded only if the instructor agrees to it
qs.ev: After that, it receives a zero.
qs.x: The penalty of 10% a day applies only up to three days; after that the work gets zero. Forty percent is the tempting calculation, but the rule stops at day three.

qs.q: What condition applies to extensions?
o: The request must be made before the work is due
The student must provide a letter from an employer
They are limited to three days per assignment
They can be granted after the deadline for good reasons
qs.ev: as long as you ask before the deadline
qs.x: Extensions (one per course, up to five days) must be requested before the deadline. Colette says that afterwards the instructor cannot grant one “even with a good reason”.

qs.q: What should Arjun do if his laptop fails the system check?
o: Buy a new webcam before the week of the exam
Take the exam without the proctoring software
Reserve a space to write the exam at the college
Ask the instructor to supervise him by phone instead
qs.ev: you can book one of the exam rooms on campus instead
qs.x: He can book an exam room on campus, preferably early because they fill up. Buying a webcam is never suggested, and the exam is always supervised.

qs.q: If Arjun withdraws during the second week, how much will he get back?
o: All of his tuition minus thirty dollars
Nothing, but he may transfer to a later session
Thirty dollars less than half the tuition
Fifty percent of what he paid
qs.ev: During the second week, you’ll get half the tuition back.
qs.x: Second-week withdrawal returns half the tuition. The $30 fee applies only to first-week refunds, and the transfer option is for withdrawals after week two.

qs.q: What is Colette’s view of the transfer option for Arjun?
o: She thinks he is unlikely to qualify for it
She sees it as useful protection given his job
She advises him to transfer before the course begins
She warns that it is available only after week four
qs.ev: Honestly, with a shift schedule, that’s a pretty good safety net.
qs.x: She calls it “a pretty good safety net” for someone working shifts. Week four was Arjun’s own example; the real condition is having submitted no more than two assignments.

parts.context: You will hear a local news report.

lines: One month after its launch, the city’s new FixIt app has been downloaded more than forty thousand times, far exceeding the city’s goal of fifteen thousand by the end of the year. The free app allows residents to report potholes, broken streetlights, graffiti and missed garbage pickups by taking a photo, which is automatically tagged with the location.

But the app’s popularity has created a problem of its own. The city received almost nine thousand reports in the first four weeks, roughly triple the number that usually came in by phone and email over the same period. Officials say a large share are duplicates, with dozens of people reporting the same pothole on busy streets.
Owen Pratt, the city’s director of digital services, says the volume caught his team off guard.

We planned for success, just not this much of it. Frankly, it’s a good problem to have. It tells us people want to be involved. But I won’t pretend the response times have been where we want them. Some reports have been sitting for two or three weeks, and that’s frustrating for residents who expected the app to make things faster.

The city says an update next week will show residents whether an issue has already been reported nearby, allowing them to add their support to the existing report instead of filing a new one. Repairs will also be prioritized partly by the number of residents supporting each report.

Not everyone is pleased with that change. Councillor Beatrice Okonjo, who represents the city’s east end, warns that it could put older neighbourhoods at a disadvantage, since fewer residents there use smartphones. She has asked staff to report back on whether phone and email reports will be given equal weight.
That’s a fair concern, and it’s exactly why the phone line isn’t going anywhere. Every report counts, however it reaches us.
The city plans to publish monthly data on response times starting in January.

qs.q: What does the report say about the number of downloads?
o: It is slightly below what the city expected for its first month
It has already gone well beyond the city’s target
It is about triple the number of phone reports
It matches the number of reports received so far
qs.ev: far exceeding the city’s goal of fifteen thousand
qs.x: Forty thousand downloads in a month far exceeds the year-end goal of fifteen thousand. “Triple” describes the number of reports compared with phone and email, not downloads.

qs.q: What problem has the app created?
o: Photos are often tagged with the wrong location
Residents have stopped calling the city by phone
Staff are overwhelmed by many repeated reports
Potholes are being repaired in the wrong order by crews
qs.ev: a large share are duplicates
qs.x: Reports tripled and many are duplicates of the same problem, which slows responses. Location tagging is described as automatic, with no errors mentioned.

qs.q: How does Owen Pratt feel about the situation?
o: He blames residents for submitting too many reports
He is confident response times are already acceptable
He thinks the app should be paused until the update is ready
He is pleased by the interest but admits delays
qs.ev: Frankly, it’s a good problem to have.
qs.x: He welcomes the public’s involvement but admits response times are not where they should be. He does not blame residents or suggest pausing the app.

qs.q: What will the update allow residents to do?
o: Back an existing report rather than make a new one
Track the crews repairing potholes on their street
Report problems by phone directly through the app
Vote on which neighbourhoods receive repairs first each month
qs.ev: allowing them to add their support to the existing report instead of filing a new one
qs.x: Residents will be able to support a report already filed nearby. Support counts will influence priority, but residents do not vote on neighbourhoods.

qs.q: Why is Councillor Okonjo concerned?
o: The app has not been translated into enough languages
Response times in the east end have been the slowest in the whole city
Some areas may get less attention because of the new ranking
Older residents are unable to download the app at all
qs.ev: it could put older neighbourhoods at a disadvantage, since fewer residents there use smartphones
qs.x: Ranking repairs by app support could favour areas with more smartphone users. She does not say east-end response times are already the slowest.

parts.context: Three members of a condominium board are discussing whether to install security cameras.

lines: Okay, last item tonight: security. Since September, we’ve had three bikes stolen from the parking garage, and someone forced open two mailboxes. I’ve had more complaints about this than about the elevator, which is saying something. I’d like us to approve cameras in every common area – the garage, the mailroom, the lobby and the hallway on each floor. The quote from Brightguard is fourteen thousand dollars.
Honestly, I’m all for it. My neighbour’s bike was one of the ones taken. If cameras make people think twice, I’d say that’s money well spent.

Can I be the difficult one for a minute? I don’t have a problem with the garage or the mailroom. But cameras in the hallways are a different matter. They’d record who visits whom, what time people come home, who’s staying over. That’s a lot of information about people’s private lives, sitting on a hard drive somewhere.
Nobody’s going to be watching the footage for fun, Devendra. It would only be checked if something happened.

That’s what everyone says at the start. But right now we don’t have any rules about who can view it or how long it’s kept. And I checked our bylaws. Recording in the residential hallways would need an amendment, which means a two-thirds vote of the owners.
Hmm. Two-thirds. We can barely get a quorum at the AGM. Speaking of which, Gloria, where would the fourteen thousand come from? The reserve fund is already committed to the roof next year.
It would probably mean a special assessment. Something like a hundred and eighty dollars per unit.
Then I take back what I said about money well spent. A lot of owners here are retired. A surprise bill of a hundred and eighty dollars for cameras in the hallways would go over terribly.
All right, all right. What if we drop the hallways and the lobby, and do just the garage and the mailroom? That brings it down to about six and a half thousand.

That I could support, on one condition: we put a written policy in place first. Only the property manager can view the footage, it’s deleted after thirty days unless there’s an incident, and there are signs posted so people know they’re being recorded.
I can live with that. It’s reasonable.

Can I suggest something cheaper we could do right away? The garage door takes almost a minute to close. Half the time, I bet the thieves are just walking in behind a car. The building manager told me a faster motor would cost about twenty-two hundred.

That’s a good point, and it comes out of the regular maintenance budget, so we don’t need an owners’ vote. Let’s do both: approve the door repair tonight, and bring the camera proposal for the garage and mailroom to the AGM in March.
I’ll draft the privacy policy so it can go out with the AGM package.
And I’ll get two more quotes for the cameras. Brightguard shouldn’t be the only company we ask, especially for a job this size.
Perfect. Do I have a motion to approve the garage door repair? Devendra, would you like to move it?

qs.q: Why does Gloria raise the issue of security?
o: The elevator was damaged during a break-in last fall
A security company offered the building a discount
Owners voted to install cameras at the last general meeting
Recent thefts have led to many complaints
qs.ev: I’ve had more complaints about this than about the elevator
qs.x: Bike thefts and mailbox break-ins have produced more complaints than the elevator. The elevator is only a comparison, and Brightguard gave a quote, not a discount.

qs.q: What is Devendra’s main objection to the original plan?
o: Hallway cameras would reveal too much about residents’ lives
Cameras in the garage would not stop bike thefts
The quote from Brightguard is far higher than other companies’ quotes
The footage would be watched by residents for fun
qs.ev: That’s a lot of information about people’s private lives
qs.x: He accepts garage and mailroom cameras but objects to hallway recording because of privacy. Watching “for fun” is Gloria’s phrase, and no other quotes have been obtained yet.

qs.q: What does Devendra point out about the bylaws?
o: They forbid cameras anywhere inside the building
They require the property manager to approve recordings
Hallway recording would need the support of most owners
They allow footage to be kept for a maximum of thirty days
qs.ev: which means a two-thirds vote of the owners
qs.x: Recording in hallways requires a bylaw amendment passed by two-thirds of owners. Thirty days and the property manager come from his proposed policy, not the current bylaws.

qs.q: Why does Sean change his mind about the original plan?
o: He learns his neighbour’s bike was recovered
He expects owners to object to an unexpected charge
He agrees with Devendra about privacy in hallways
He thinks the roof repair should be delayed instead of the cameras
qs.ev: A surprise bill of a hundred and eighty dollars for cameras in the hallways would go over terribly.
qs.x: Once he hears about a $180 special assessment, he withdraws “money well spent” because many owners are retired. His change is about cost, not privacy.

qs.q: What is Gloria’s attitude toward Devendra’s conditions?
o: She finds them acceptable
She thinks they will delay the project too much
She accepts them only for the garage cameras
She believes the manager should not view any footage
qs.ev: I can live with that. It’s reasonable.
qs.x: “I can live with that. It’s reasonable” shows acceptance. Her earlier remark about nobody watching for fun was before the reduced plan, and she raises no concern about delay.

qs.q: Why does Sean suggest the garage door repair?
o: The building manager has refused to install cameras there
The door was damaged during one of the recent thefts
It would remove the need for any cameras at all in the garage
It addresses a likely way thieves are getting in
qs.ev: Half the time, I bet the thieves are just walking in behind a car.
qs.x: The slow door may let thieves walk in behind cars, so a faster motor tackles the cause cheaply. They still plan to propose garage cameras, so it does not replace them.

qs.q: Why can the door repair be approved tonight?
o: Owners already voted for it at the last AGM
It is paid from a budget that needs no owner vote
It costs less than the reserve fund holds for the roof
The building manager has already ordered the new motor for it
qs.ev: it comes out of the regular maintenance budget, so we don’t need an owners’ vote
qs.x: Because it is a regular maintenance expense, the board can approve it without owners. The reserve fund is committed to the roof and is not the source.

qs.q: What will happen at the AGM in March?
o: Owners will vote on cameras in every common area of the building
Sean will present only the original Brightguard quote
A reduced camera plan will be put to the owners
Devendra will ask owners to amend the hallway bylaw
qs.ev: bring the camera proposal for the garage and mailroom to the AGM in March
qs.x: Only garage and mailroom cameras go to the AGM, so no hallway bylaw change is needed. Sean will seek two more quotes rather than rely on Brightguard alone.

parts.context: You will hear a reporter presenting different views on a proposed “right to disconnect” law.

lines: Since the pandemic, the line between the office and the kitchen table has all but disappeared for many Canadians. Now, a proposal in the provincial legislature would require employers with more than twenty-five staff to adopt a written ‘right to disconnect’ policy, setting out when employees are expected not to answer emails, messages or calls about work. Supporters see it as long-overdue protection. Others think it misunderstands how modern work actually happens.

Labour researcher Dr. Simone Achari, whose team surveyed more than two thousand remote and hybrid workers last year, says the numbers are hard to ignore. Six in ten respondents said they checked work messages after nine p.m. at least three times a week, and most said they did so not because they were asked to, but because they worried about appearing less committed than their colleagues. In her view, that’s precisely why a policy is needed: the pressure isn’t written down anywhere, so it can’t be challenged.

But critics point out that the proposal says very little about what a policy must contain. A company could technically comply by writing a single paragraph that changes nothing. Achari acknowledges this, but argues that even a vague policy gives workers something concrete to point to when they push back.
For small business owners, the concerns are different. Luc Thibodeau runs a software company with thirty-two employees, most of whom work remotely across four time zones.

My team in Halifax starts work when my developers in Vancouver are still asleep. If someone in Halifax sends a message at four in the afternoon, it lands in Vancouver at noon, fine. But the reply sometimes comes back to Halifax at eight at night. Who’s in the wrong there? I’m not against the idea. I just don’t want a rule written for a nine-to-five office in one city applied to a company that never really closes.

Thibodeau says his company already uses a simpler approach: messages sent outside someone’s working hours are scheduled to arrive the next morning, and nobody is expected to answer them until then. He’d prefer the government encourage practical tools like that rather than require policies on paper.

Some workers I spoke to were also lukewarm. A nurse who works remotely as a scheduling coordinator told me she actually prefers answering a few messages in the evening, because it means she can leave early to pick up her kids. A rigid rule, she said, might take away the flexibility that made remote work attractive in the first place.
The bill goes to second reading in the spring.

qs.q: What would the proposed law require?
o: Bigger employers must set out rules on after-hours contact
All employees must stop answering emails after nine p.m.
Companies must pay staff for checking messages in the evening
Remote workers must keep fixed hours in one time zone
qs.ev: would require employers with more than twenty-five staff to adopt a written ‘right to disconnect’ policy
qs.x: Employers with over 25 staff would need a written policy on when workers need not respond. Nine p.m. comes from the survey results, not from the bill.

qs.q: According to Dr. Achari’s survey, why do many workers check messages late?
o: Their managers specifically ask them to stay available
They fear looking less dedicated than co-workers
They prefer to finish work after their children are asleep
Their colleagues work in several other time zones
qs.ev: because they worried about appearing less committed than their colleagues
qs.x: Most said they were not asked to; they worried about seeming less committed. Time zones are Thibodeau’s issue, and children relate to the nurse’s story.

qs.q: How does Achari respond to criticism that the law is vague?
o: She agrees that it should be withdrawn and rewritten
She says details will be added after second reading
She denies that companies could comply with one paragraph

p1.meta: From: Bethany Rourke  |  To: Ines Castellano  |  Subject: Greetings from the edge of the map
p1.text:
Hi Ines,

It’s been almost a year since I packed up my desk at Halberd & Pike and drove east, so I figured I owed you more than a “like” on your vacation photos.

The short version: I love it here, mostly. Cape Mirelle has about nine hundred people, one grocery store, and a view from my kitchen window that I still haven’t gotten used to. Working remotely has been easier than I expected in some ways and harder in others. The work itself is fine – our team meetings were on video anyway, and I get far more done without the open-plan chatter. The internet, on the other hand, has been an adventure. When a storm comes through, it can go down for a whole day, so I’ve learned to keep a mobile hotspot charged and to warn my manager whenever the forecast looks bad.

The harder part, which I didn’t see coming, is how quiet the days are. In the city, I complained constantly about interruptions. Now I sometimes realize at four o’clock that I haven’t said a word out loud since breakfast. I joined the curling club in November mainly to have a reason to leave the house, and to my surprise, I’m not terrible at it.

Now for the real reason I’m writing. Head office is holding a planning retreat in Toronto the week of March 9, and they’ve asked me to attend in person. While I’m there, they also want to talk to me about a team lead position. The catch is that it would require me to be in the office three days a week. I honestly don’t know how I feel about that. I miss people, but I don’t miss the commute, or the rent.

Two favours, then. Could I stay on your sofa for those five nights? The company will pay for a hotel, but I’d much rather catch up with you properly. And could you be my sounding board? You went back to the office full-time last year after working from home, and you’re the only person I know who has done it in that direction.

Let me know if March works. I’ll bring a jar of bakeapple jam as payment.

Bethany

p3.title: Game On: Esports Enter the High School
paras: When Dario Pellerin, a math teacher at Kestrel Lake Secondary, started an esports club in 2019, he had six students and no budget. The team practised after school on four computers borrowed from the school library, which were so slow that matches occasionally froze halfway through. Pellerin had started the club almost by accident, after noticing that several of his quietest students spent lunch hour discussing strategy for an online team game. Many of them, he realized, had never joined a single club or team in all their years at the school. Today, the program has grown to more than eighty students playing on five teams, and Kestrel Lake competes in a provincial high school league that now includes forty schools. Matches are played online during the week, with an in-person championship held each spring in a university gymnasium.

Supporters argue that the benefits go well beyond entertainment. Competitive team games require players to communicate under pressure, divide up roles and adjust their plans quickly when something goes wrong. Coaches at Kestrel Lake spend as much time reviewing recordings of matches with students as they do on actual play, pointing out moments when a lack of communication cost the team. The school’s guidance counsellor, Helen Marchetti, has noticed another change: since joining the club, a number of students who were frequently absent now rarely miss class, because practice is held right after the last bell. A small number of colleges in Canada and the United States have also started offering scholarships to skilled esports players, which has caught the attention of parents who were initially skeptical of the whole idea.

Not every parent has been won over, however. The most common concern is screen time, particularly for teenagers who already spend hours on their phones. Others worry about the content of popular games, some of which involve realistic violence. The provincial league has tried to address both issues. It allows only team strategy games and sports simulations, and it bans titles that are rated for adults. Practice is limited to six hours a week, and every session at Kestrel Lake begins with stretching and includes short breaks to rest players’ eyes and wrists. Students must also maintain a passing grade in every course to remain on a team, a rule Pellerin says he enforces strictly. Two of his best players were benched last semester until they had caught up in chemistry.

Money remains a challenge. A computer powerful enough to run competitive games costs about $2,000, and the school board does not fund equipment for extracurricular activities. Kestrel Lake paid for its current machines through a sponsorship from a local internet provider and a fundraising tournament that drew teams from across the region. Organizers are also trying to change the makeup of the league. At present, only about fifteen percent of players are girls, and a separate division for girls is being discussed for next season. Some teachers would like esports to go further still, becoming a for-credit course that covers topics such as game design and digital citizenship. The provincial education ministry has said it is watching the programs with interest but has not committed to any changes in the curriculum.

p4.title: Too Many Apps, Not Enough Communication
p4.byline: Opinion | by Harriet Mwangi, parent and former school council chair
p4.text:
Last month, I missed my son’s parent-teacher interview. Not because I forgot, and not because I was too busy, but because the booking link was sent through an app I didn’t know his school had started using. By the time a friend mentioned it at pickup, every slot was gone.

I have three children in two schools, and at last count I had six different apps on my phone to keep track of them. One for attendance. One for homework and grades. One for paying for field trips and pizza days. One for the school newsletter. One that some teachers use for messages, and another that other teachers prefer. Each sends its own notifications, in its own style, at its own times. On a typical school day, my phone buzzes more than twenty times with updates about my children’s education, and I would estimate that fewer than three of them require me to do anything.

The result is predictable. Like most parents I know, I have started ignoring the notifications altogether. And that is exactly when the important ones – the interview booking, the permission form due tomorrow, the change to early dismissal – slip through.

I want to be fair. Some of these tools are genuinely useful. Getting a message within minutes when my daughter is marked absent is a real improvement over finding out at the end of the week. Paying online for a field trip is easier than sending a cheque in a sandwich bag. Nobody is asking schools to go back to paper.

But the current situation is not a communication system. It is a pile of separate decisions, each sensible on its own, that together create noise. Individual teachers choose the app they like. Schools sign contracts with different companies. Nobody seems to be responsible for asking what it all looks like from the kitchen table.

The cost is not only frustration. Families without reliable internet, parents who are new to Canada and still learning English, and grandparents raising grandchildren are the most likely to fall through the cracks. A system that works only for the most tech-savvy parents is not a fair one.

Teachers pay a price too. Several have told me they now post the same announcement in three places, and that parents message them at ten o’clock at night expecting an immediate answer. That is time that should be going into lessons.

So here is what I would propose. First, each school board should choose one platform for all communication with families and require every school to use it. Second, non-urgent updates should be bundled into a single weekly summary, sent on the same day each week. Third, anything genuinely urgent – a lockdown, an early closure – should come by phone call or text as well, so it reaches everyone. And finally, boards should make clear that teachers are not expected to reply to messages outside school hours.

None of this requires new technology or a bigger budget. It requires someone to take responsibility for the whole picture. Until that happens, I will keep scrolling through twenty notifications a day, hoping I don’t miss the one that matters.

t1.situation: Two months ago, you switched to a cheaper monthly plan with your mobile phone provider after speaking with a customer service agent by phone. However, your last two bills have charged you the old, higher price, and you were also charged a fee that the agent never mentioned.
bullets: Explain what you agreed to when you changed your plan

t1.model:
Dear Customer Service Team,

I am writing about billing errors on my account, number 4417-2290.

On August 28, I called your support line and spoke with an agent named Kevin, who switched me from the Unlimited Plus plan at $85 per month to the Essentials 20 plan at $55 per month. He confirmed that the change would take effect immediately and that there would be no fees, since I had completed my two-year contract. I also received a confirmation text that afternoon.

t2.intro: Your company is deciding how employees will work next year and has asked all staff to complete a short survey.
t2.question: Which option do you prefer? Explain the reasons for your choice.
t2.a: Option A: All employees work in the office on the same three fixed days each week (Tuesday to Thursday) and from home on the other two days.
t2.b: Option B: All employees work fully from home, and the company holds a paid three-day in-person gathering for everyone every three months.
t2.model:
I would choose Option A, three fixed office days each week.

Although working fully from home is convenient, I believe our team has lost something important since we stopped seeing each other regularly. Many of our best ideas used to come from quick conversations at someone’s desk, and those simply do not happen on video calls, which tend to be scheduled and formal. Having everyone in the office on the same days would bring those conversations back.

Another advantage is support for newer staff. Our department has hired six people this year, and several have told me they find it hard to learn the job when they cannot watch experienced colleagues or ask a quick question. A gathering every three months would be enjoyable, but it would not provide the daily guidance new employees need.

Of course, Option B would save commuting time and money. However, with two days at home each week, Option A still offers much of that flexibility, and fixed days would make it easier to plan childcare and appointments.

For these reasons, I believe Option A offers the better balance for our team.

t1.prompt: Your friend’s 11-year-old daughter is asking for her first smartphone because most of her classmates have one. Your friend is unsure what to do. Advise your friend.
t1.model: I completely understand why you’re torn. Eleven feels young, but you also don’t want her to be the only kid left out of every group chat. Here’s what I’d suggest. First, think about what she actually needs a phone for. If it’s mainly to reach you after school and message a few friends, she doesn’t need a full smartphone right away. There are basic phones, or even smartwatches for kids, that let her call and text without access to social media or the whole internet. Second, if you do decide on a smartphone, set the rules before she gets it, not after. Agree on things like where the phone sleeps at night – ideally outside her bedroom – and which apps she’s allowed to download. Some families even write a simple contract and both sign it. Third, use the parental controls. Most phones let you set time limits and approve downloads, and you can loosen them gradually as she shows she’s responsible. Finally, talk to the other parents in her class. You might find that fewer kids have phones than she claims, or that some families would like to agree on a common approach. That way, she won’t feel singled out, and you won’t feel like the strict parent.

t2.prompt: Talk about a time when you learned something useful by watching videos or taking a course online. What did you learn, and how did it help you?
t2.model: Last winter, my kitchen faucet started leaking, and the plumber I called couldn’t come for over a week. Out of frustration, I decided to watch a few online videos to see if I could fix it myself. I found a really clear one by a retired plumber who explained every step slowly and showed exactly which parts to buy. I went to the hardware store with a photo of my faucet, bought a replacement part for about fifteen dollars, and followed the video one step at a time. It took me almost two hours, partly because I kept pausing and rewinding, but it worked perfectly. I was so proud of myself. Since then, I’ve fixed a running toilet the same way. It saved me money, but more importantly, it gave me the confidence that I can learn practical skills on my own.

t3.prompt: Describe some things that are happening in the picture as well as you can. The person you are speaking to cannot see the picture.
t3.model: This is a busy outdoor market on what looks like a sunny weekend morning. On the left, there’s a stall with a blue sign that says “Phone Repair.” A man with glasses, in a blue shirt, is standing in front of it holding a phone, and a teenage girl in a pink top is holding out her own phone, probably asking him to fix it. In the middle, there’s a yellow sign that says “Free Phone Charging,” and a woman in a teal top is walking past it pushing a stroller. Just in front of her, a man in a dark shirt is taking photos with a camera, and a brown dog is standing nearby. On the right, there’s a green stall that says “Farm Fresh,” where a woman in an orange dress is holding a bag, and another shopper in purple is walking away.

t4.prompt: In this picture, what do you think will most probably happen next?
t4.model: I think the man at the phone repair stall is going to take the girl’s phone and look at the screen, and he’ll probably tell her it needs a new battery or a new screen. If it’s a quick job, she might decide to wait, so she could wander over to the farm stall in the meantime. The man with the camera seems interested in the market, so I expect he’ll keep taking pictures, maybe of the colourful stalls or of the dog, which will probably trot over to sniff the stroller. The woman with the stroller might stop at the farm stall to buy some vegetables, or she may even plug her phone in at the charging station. And the shopper in purple, who’s already carrying a bag, will most likely head home. Overall, I think the market will get even busier as the morning goes on.

t5.intro: You want to make your family’s home more secure after several break-ins in your neighbourhood. You have found two options. Choose the option that you prefer. In the next section, you will need to persuade a family member that your choice is better than the one they prefer.

options.title: Smart camera kit
details: $390 for a doorbell camera and 2 outdoor cameras
Live video and alerts on your phone
Works only when the Wi-Fi is on

options.title: Monitored alarm system
details: Staff call police if the alarm goes off

other.title: Motion lights and stronger locks
details: Lights turn on when someone approaches

t5.persuade: Your father prefers motion lights and stronger locks. Persuade him that your choice is better.
t5.model: Dad, I agree that motion lights and better locks are a smart start, and I love that there are no monthly fees. But I really think the smart camera kit gives us much more protection. The main problem with lights and locks is that we’d never know if someone tried to get in. With the cameras, we get an alert on our phones the moment someone comes near the door, and we can actually see who it is, even when we’re at work or away at the cottage. If something did happen, we’d have video for the police and the insurance company. Lights don’t give you any evidence. Yes, there’s an eight-dollar monthly fee for recording, but that’s less than two coffees. And it only takes an hour to set up – I can do it myself this weekend.

t6.situation: In a private chat with a coworker, you complained about a decision your manager made. This morning, you discovered that the coworker had shared a screenshot of your message in the team’s group chat, where your manager could see it. Your coworker says it was an accident.
options: Talk to your coworker and explain how this has affected you.
Talk to your manager and explain the message she may have seen.
t6.note: Choose ONE option and speak to that person.
t6.model: Hi Teresa, thanks for making time. I wanted to talk to you directly about the screenshot that was posted in the team chat this morning. I’m guessing you saw it. First, I want to apologize. I wrote that message in a private conversation after a frustrating day, and the way I expressed myself wasn’t professional. I’m sorry it ended up in front of the whole team. That said, I’d like to explain the concern behind it, because I think it’s a fair one. When the project deadline was moved up by two weeks, I worried that we didn’t have enough people to do the testing properly. I should have brought that to you instead of venting. From now on, I’ll raise issues with you directly. And if it helps, I’m happy to go over the testing schedule with you today.

t7.prompt: Answer the following question: Should parents use phone apps to track the location of their teenage children? Explain your reasons.
t7.model: I think location tracking can be a reasonable tool for parents, but only if it’s done openly and with the teenager’s agreement. Let me explain why. On the positive side, it can genuinely improve safety. If a teenager misses their curfew or doesn’t answer their phone, being able to see that they’re at a friend’s house rather than stranded somewhere can save parents a lot of worry, and it can help in a real emergency. Many teens actually appreciate it too, for example when they need a ride home late at night. However, I’m strongly against secret tracking. If teenagers discover that their parents have been watching their every move without telling them, it can seriously damage trust, and they may simply leave their phone at a friend’s place or find ways to switch the app off. Teenagers also need some privacy to develop independence and learn to make their own decisions. So, in my opinion, the best approach is transparency. Parents should explain why they want to use the app, agree on when it will be checked – maybe only if the teen is late or unreachable – and gradually turn it off as the teenager gets older. Used that way, it’s a safety net rather than surveillance.

scene.alt: A furnished apartment living room where almost the entire back wall is covered by one gigantic television, much taller than a person and about three metres wide. The screen shows the words “WELCOME HOME” in large white letters. In front of it is a small red sofa that looks tiny by comparison, and a man in a blue shirt sits on it holding a mug, looking up at the screen. On the left, a real estate agent in a green shirt stands by a window and points at the TV, and a grey cat sits on the floor. On the right are a small wooden chair, a floor lamp, a potted plant and a clock on the wall.

t8.prompt: You are looking for an apartment to share with a roommate, and you have found this furnished apartment online. Call your roommate, describe the living room, and explain whether you think you should rent it. Your roommate cannot see the picture.
t8.model: Hi Sam, I just found a furnished two-bedroom that you have to hear about. The strangest thing is the living room. Almost the entire back wall is one gigantic TV screen – I mean it’s easily three metres wide, from near the floor almost to the ceiling. In the photo, it says “Welcome Home” in huge white letters. In front of it, there’s a red sofa that looks tiny by comparison, and someone’s sitting on it with a mug, staring up at the screen. There’s also a grey cat, a floor lamp, a plant and a little wooden chair. Honestly, I’m not sure we should take it. It would be amazing for movie nights, but I bet the electricity bill would be huge, and you’d practically need to sit in the hallway to see the whole screen. Also, there’s no room for a dining table.
